tldr: This paper presents a framework that uses a GPU physics simulator as an online world model and embeds a quadratic programming (QP) projection—accounting for joint jerk limits—directly into the sampling loop, enabling real-time bimanual contact manipulation in cluttered environments without demonstration data.
hero_caption: System architecture tightly coupling real hardware and simulation. Dynamic object poses measured by OptiTrack are streamed to MuJoCo via ROS 2, while parallel rollouts and Model Predictive Control (MPC) run in real time on a laptop GPU.
overview:
Coordinated dual-arm manipulation is a powerful approach for supporting or pinching and carrying large objects. However, planning contact-rich motions remains extremely challenging. Recently, end-to-end learning methods such as imitation learning have become mainstream, but they require massive demonstration datasets and suffer from a fundamental fragility: they readily fail under distribution shifts, such as changes in obstacle placement.

To tackle this, the authors focus on Model Predictive Control (MPC) that directly leverages a GPU-accelerated physics simulator (MuJoCo) as an online "world model" rather than training an entire deep model. Yet, conventional sampling-based MPC algorithms like MPPI and CEM face an inherent trade-off: widening exploration causes aggressive control oscillations that violate robot limits, while restricting exploration to smooth commands causes the planner to get trapped in local minima.

To resolve this dilemma, the authors propose PRISM. Before evaluating sampled joint-velocity trajectories in physics simulation, PRISM applies a minimum-correction projection via quadratic programming (QP) so that trajectories strictly satisfy position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk limits, along with boundary continuity for MPC. This allows bold, wide-ranging exploration while ensuring that only smooth, kinematically executable motions are evaluated. Furthermore, task-specific cost weights are automatically tuned offline using Bayesian optimization.

Experiments evaluate four contact-rich tasks in cluttered environments: tray transport, ball pinching transport, cube handover, and box lifting. PRISM achieves significantly higher success rates (up to 95–100%) compared to existing sampling-based baselines, and successfully transfers to physical dual UR5e manipulators.
contributions: Integrated a GPU-parallel QP projection into sampling-based MPC that simultaneously enforces joint position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk limits, as well as MPC boundary continuity, completely reconciling broad exploration with motion smoothness.

Designed a custom ADMM/Bregman-splitting solver exploiting joint-wise separability and precomputed Cholesky factorizations, keeping the projection's computational overhead negligible compared to the full physics simulation.

Established a multi-phase cost function design for contact-rich bimanual tasks (such as pinching transport and aerial handover), accompanied by an offline Bayesian optimization pipeline to automatically tune cost weights.
Demonstrated real-time physical dual-arm control at 10–16 Hz on a single laptop GPU using OptiTrack and MuJoCo/MJX in real-world environments featuring unseen obstacle layouts.

sections.heading: From data-heavy imitation learning to online planning with physics simulators
sections.summary: Dual-arm robots are key to reproducing human dexterity, but conventional imitation learning struggles in unseen scenarios like shifted obstacles. This work introduces PRISM, a novel MPC framework that runs a GPU-accelerated physics simulator online as a world model and reconciles smoothness with exploration via QP projection.
sections.details:
Dual-arm manipulation is highly promising for assembly and logistics automation because it enables grasping large objects and applying opposing forces beyond the reach of single-arm systems. However, mainstream imitation learning and reinforcement learning paradigms, while bypassing explicit contact modeling, rely heavily on extensive training data variations. A slight displacement of an obstacle can easily break their execution, requiring additional data collection or fine-tuning.

This limitation has brought attention back to Model Predictive Control (MPC) running a GPU-parallel physics simulator online as an internal model. Because it directly evaluates the current scene's geometric and physical state, it can adapt immediately to unseen obstacle arrangements.

PRISM embeds a quadratic programming (QP) projection directly into the sampling-based MPC exploration loop. At each control step, joint-velocity trajectories drawn from an adaptive Gaussian distribution are instantly projected onto a kinematically feasible set satisfying position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk limits. Consequently, without relying on post-hoc smoothing filters or soft penalties, the optimizer can explore with aggressive variance while evaluating only smooth, physically safe trajectories in parallel on MuJoCo.

sections.heading: How to overcome the oscillation problem in sampling-based MPC
sections.summary: While sampling-based MPC handles discontinuous contact events well, it often produces non-smooth control inputs. This section surveys the limitations of conventional workarounds—such as post-hoc filters and low-frequency sampling—and highlights the advantages of QP pre-projection.
sections.details:
Related work is structured around four main pillars:

- Sampling-based manipulation planning: Gradient-based trajectory optimization struggles with contact mode switches and cluttered environments. Sampling-based methods such as MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) and CEM (Cross Entropy Method) optimize trajectories relying solely on forward rollouts and cost evaluations. However, finding trajectories that satisfy dual-arm kinematic closed chains purely through random sampling is non-trivial.

- Ensuring smoothness in sampling-based MPC: Trajectories generated by MPPI or CEM often exhibit high-frequency chatter across time, risking actuator wear or damage on real robots. Post-hoc smoothing, like Savitzky-Golay filtering (SGF), alters trajectories after optimization and cannot guarantee physical feasibility during rollouts. Meanwhile, frequency-limiting methods like low-pass filtering (LPF-MPPI) or colored noise still violate acceleration and jerk limits when sample amplitudes are large, and they cannot guarantee velocity continuity across MPC replanning boundaries.

- Projection-based approaches: Projecting sampled trajectories onto feasible sets via minimal QP corrections (e.g., $\pi$-MPPI) is the only strategy that rigorously enforces hardware constraints while retaining large sampling variance. PRISM extends this concept to joint-space jerk limits for dual-arm systems.

- Automatic cost tuning and end-to-end learning: Tuning multi-objective and multi-phase cost weights for complex bimanual tasks has historically relied on human trial and error. PRISM automates this process using Bayesian optimization (BO).

sections.heading: The core of PRISM: A parallel QP projection algorithm bounding jerk
sections.summary: Candidate trajectories sampled from the joint-velocity space are projected simultaneously via QP to satisfy position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk limits, as well as continuity with current joint velocities. Because this QP separates across joints, it runs ultra-fast on GPUs without bottlenecking the physics simulation.
sections.details:
The overall architecture and mathematical formulation of PRISM consist of the following:

- Sampling-based optimization loop: The optimizer adopts an adaptive Gaussian distribution combining MPPI-style importance-weighted mean updates and CEM-style diagonal covariance updates. It samples joint-velocity sequences across horizon $H$ for both arms.

- QP projection formulation: For raw samples $\tilde{\dot{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}}$, the solver finds feasible trajectories $\dot{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}^*$ that minimize squared error. Positions, accelerations, and jerks are represented as linear inequalities using an Euler integration matrix $\mathbf{L}$, a first-order backward difference matrix $\mathbf{D}_1$, and a second-order backward difference matrix $\mathbf{D}_2$, respectively. Furthermore, setting an equality constraint on the first-step velocity to match the robot's measured state $\dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\mathrm{init}}$ eliminates velocity discontinuities across MPC replanning cycles.

- Complete decoupling of exploration and smoothness: Normally, enlarging sampling variance causes erratic commands, while reducing it causes premature convergence to local minima. With QP projection, the planner can explore aggressively with high variance, while the projected trajectories strictly adhere to physical limits, pushing the hardware to its envelope. In single-joint validation, the effective standard deviation $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}$ that stays within kinematic limits reached 0.4716 with QP projection, roughly a 45- to 100-fold expansion over the baseline (0.0045) and LPF (0.0106).

- Custom GPU ADMM solver: Because the QP objective and constraints are separable across joints, a 12-DoF dual-arm system can be solved as $12 \times n$ independent sub-QPs in parallel. Using an ADMM/Bregman-splitting scheme with a constant KKT matrix, the Cholesky factorization is computed only once offline. Online, the solver converges to global optimality in just 10–20 iterations through simple matrix-vector multiplications and slack variable clipping.

captions.F3: Comparison of sampled trajectories for a single joint. While the baseline (left) and LPF (center) are forced to shrink variance drastically to stay within limits, the proposed QP projection (right) matches the initial velocity and aggressively explores the entire velocity, acceleration, and jerk envelope.

sections.heading: Task-specific cost design balancing contact and geometric constraints
sections.summary: Alongside shared costs like collision avoidance and relative velocity damping for bimanual coordination, multi-phase cost functions were designed for four demanding tasks: tray transport, ball pinching, cube handover, and box lifting. Decoupling collision penalties during designated phases unlocks natural contact behaviors.
sections.details:
The shared components and task-specific designs are detailed as follows:

- Shared costs: Collision avoidance utilizes barrier-inspired repulsive terms to prevent approaching obstacle boundaries. A home-pose deviation penalty is included, along with a constraint encouraging relative end-effector velocities to remain orthogonal to their relative position vector, preventing tearing or crushing rigid objects held by both hands.

- Moving Tray: Structured into two phases: pick (approach) and move (transport). It combines end-effector height ($z$-coordinate) alignment, grasping distance constraints, and target orientation error costs for the tray to bypass obstacles while remaining level.

- Lifting and Transporting Ball: The robot lifts and carries the ball purely via friction by squeezing it between end-effectors, without parallel grippers. Critically, during the move phase, the collision cost between the ball and end-effectors is removed. This allows the physics engine to resolve intentional pushing into the ball. End-effectors are also constrained to face each other in the $yz$-plane.

- Hand-Over: Composed of four phases: pick, pass, place, and home. One arm reaches through a tight cluster of obstacles to pick the cube, synchronizes and hands it over in mid-air to the other arm, which then places it at the goal and returns home—controlling an intricate sequential task.

- Lifting and Transporting Box: Unlike a symmetric ball, a flat-sided box easily slips in rotation. Individual alignment costs are placed on each end-effector relative to the opposing faces of the box, with strict orientation costs to keep the box level across all three axes.

captions.F4: Dual-arm robot setup and shared global coordinate frame. Tasks such as ball pinching and cube handover explicitly incorporate constraints in the cost function, such as end-effector opposing alignment in the $yz$-plane.

sections.heading: Validation and benchmarking: Outperforming baselines in success and adaptability
sections.summary: PRISM was evaluated on dual UR5e manipulators and in simulation against smoothing MPC baselines like LPF, SGF, and vanilla CEM. Combining QP projection with Bayesian optimization yielded 90–100% success rates and exhibited strong online robustness to unseen obstacle layouts.
sections.details:
Key experimental results include:

- Implementation and speed: Implemented in JAX using the GPU physics engine MJX with a 0.1 s control time step. Even with high sample counts, ball transport, tray transport, and handover run under 80 ms per step, sustaining real-time control loops (10–16 Hz).

- Baseline comparisons: Evaluated against vanilla CEM, LPF-MPPI, and SGF-MPPI. Vanilla CEM suffered from severe chattering, degrading warm-starts and dropping handover success to 15%. In contrast, PRISM achieved 95% on tray transport (vs. 70% for SGF, 50% for LPF) and 90% on handover (vs. 80% for LPF, 75% for SGF). Furthermore, while LPF and SGF required heuristic workarounds—such as collision-free IK pre-alignment and extra acceleration penalties—PRISM operated reliably using only QP kinematic constraints.

- Impact of Bayesian optimization (BO): Tuning cost weights offline via 1000 BO episodes per task (3–9 hours on an RTX 4090) dramatically boosted success rates compared to manual tuning: tray transport improved from 45% to 90%, handover from 60% to 95%, and ball transport from 75% to 100%, with zero added latency during online inference.

- Comparison with imitation learning: In a Franka-Panda ball lifting scenario with an unseen obstacle, the imitation learning policy collided mid-lift and dropped to 20% success. In contrast, PRISM dynamically avoided the obstacle inside simulation, maintaining a 60% success rate.

captions.F6: Simulation (top) and hardware execution (bottom) of the ball lifting and transport task. The two arms dynamically adapt their configuration while maintaining opposing forces in the $yz$-plane as they clear a central obstacle wall.
captions.F7: Cube handover task within a cluttered environment of floating spherical obstacles. The left arm navigates around obstacles to pick up the cube, hands it off accurately in mid-air to the right arm, which then places it at the goal.
captions.F9: Performance statistics across tasks under varying batch sizes (sample counts). Success rates plateau around 1250 samples, and computation times stay within real-time limits under 80 ms, except for the complex box task.
captions.F10: Performance comparison between manual tuning and Bayesian optimization weights. Success rates improve dramatically across all tasks without increasing computation time (e.g., a 45% gain on tray transport).

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook: Unifying model-based planning and learning
sections.summary: PRISM reconciles aggressive exploration with strict smoothness via QP projection, enabling contact-rich bimanual manipulation in real time. Future directions include distilling planned trajectories into imitation policies for warm-starting MPC and integrating learned value functions for long-horizon tasks.
sections.details:
Summary and future perspectives presented by the authors:

- Summary: The authors proposed PRISM, an MPC framework combining a GPU physics simulator as a world model with an ADMM-based parallel QP projection inside the sampling loop. By strictly enforcing joint position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk limits, PRISM generates smooth trajectories without restricting exploration variance. Combined with Bayesian optimization for parameter tuning, its effectiveness was demonstrated on physical dual-arm contact manipulation tasks.

- Limitations: While cost weights can be tuned via Bayesian optimization, designing the cost terms and partitioning the task into phases still relies on manual engineering. Additionally, PRISM depends on MuJoCo's physics fidelity, meaning sim-to-real gaps could emerge in tasks involving deformable bodies, fluids, or highly dynamic frictional transitions.

- Future directions: One promising path is distilling trajectories generated by PRISM into reactive policy networks to warm-start MPC, drastically cutting down required sampling iterations. Another avenue is incorporating learned value functions as terminal costs (similar to TD-MPC) to plan over much longer task horizons.

takeaways: The fundamental conflict between exploration breadth and control smoothness in sampling-based MPC is resolved by applying a least-squares QP projection prior to rollout evaluation.
Leveraging joint-wise separability in an ADMM solver allows QP projections with acceleration and jerk bounds to parallelize on GPUs without creating a compute bottleneck.
In contact-rich manipulation, a multi-phase cost design that selectively disables collision penalties with the target object during designated contact phases proves highly effective.
Offline Bayesian optimization over randomized task conditions automatically tunes MPC cost weights, significantly boosting success rates without adding runtime computational overhead.
limitations: Structuring task phases (such as approach and transport) and determining which geometric constraints and error terms belong in each phase still relies on manual engineering.
The framework assumes access to an accurate MuJoCo physics model, preventing direct application to deformable objects like cloth or ropes, or unknown objects with drastically fluctuating friction.
In delicate tasks prone to rotational slip—such as pinching asymmetric boxes—the success rate remains around 80%, with higher computation times than simpler tasks.
